$SPY Monday and Tuesday played out pretty much as expected: mostly noise and chop while the market waited for today.

I’m watching price, oil, DXY and yields, but today’s real information comes from the Fed decision at 2:00 and Warsh at 2:30.

The market is overwhelmingly pricing a 25bp hike. My personal prediction remains the same, I think Warsh could surprise the market and hold.

But my prediction and my trade are two different things. I’m not gambling on the decision beforehand.

If Warsh holds, I expect an initial bullish reaction because a hold would surprise current market pricing. I’d also expect DXY and yields, particularly the 2Y, to weaken as confirmation. Then I want to hear Warsh.

If it’s a dovish/data dependent hold and the market likes the press conference, we could squeeze hard and potentially put ATHs back in play. A dovish hold in this current environment is very unlikely but anything is possible.

If SPY rips today however, I’m not chasing it.
In fact, the stronger today’s move higher is, the more interested I become in a pullback/reversal afterward.

If Wednesday closes strongly green, I’ll consider Thursday for the FOMC flip. A pullback could be temporary before another push higher, or, if the rally becomes exhausted around the highs, it could start developing into the larger correction I’ve been waiting for.

If instead we get a hawkish hold and SPY dumps, I’ll let it sell. If we flush toward 749–751 and buyers defend it, I’d become interested in calls for the flip reversal.

If Warsh hikes and this is what the market expects. I’d watch for DXY and the 2Y to strengthen, while the long end may react differently depending on how the hike is interpreted.

If SPY sells off hard, I’m not chasing puts.
Quite the opposite. The harder the initial FOMC flush, the more interested I become in the rebound afterward.

If support confirms, particularly around 749–751, I’d look for calls late Wednesday or Thursday for a potentially strong bounce over the following sessions.

If instead we get a dovish/one and done hike and SPY rallies hard, I won’t chase that either. I’ll wait for the move to exhaust and look for the pullback.

This is the important part: The bigger the initial FOMC move, the more interested I am in the move that comes AFTER it.

If FOMC sends SPY sharply lower today, I think that could set up a strong rebound afterward potentially before the larger correction.

If FOMC sends SPY sharply higher today, I think the risk increasingly shifts toward the opposite move afterward, first through the FOMC flip/pullback, and potentially into the larger decline if buyers become exhausted near the highs. That will all depend on how price reacts after the first pull back, and whether it hold key supports or not.

A hold will signal a move for ATHs, and a breakdown will signal the next leg lower is about to begin.

So I’m not trying to predict the exact candle sequence. I’m just trying to prepare myself to react correctly to whatever outcome we get.

Busy days ahead of us💸💸

Investors are no longer hedging against a tech stock crash.

The average 1-month put-to-call skew of the Nasdaq 100 index is down to 0 points, its 4th-lowest reading over the last 20 years.

This measures how much more investors are paying for downside protection through put options than for upside exposure through call options, with the current reading indicating historically low demand for Nasdaq put options.

This figure has dropped -0.25 points since March 2026, one of the largest 6-month declines on record.

By comparison, the long-term average of this metric is 0.11 points.

Meanwhile, the cost of options used to bet on or protect against large moves in the average Nasdaq 100 stock fell sharply last week, with 1-month implied volatility dropping -17 percentage points, to ~40%.

Investors are extremely bullish on tech.
